title: TEXTBEFORE, TEXTAFTER, TEXTSPLIT & TEXTJOIN
goal: Cut text at a separator with TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER, predict what TEXTSPLIT spills, and join a list into one cell with TEXTJOIN or &.

steps.text:
In Topic 28 you cut an email at the `@` with FIND and LEFT. It worked, but it was a mouthful.

Microsoft 365 (and Excel 2024) has shortcuts: **TEXTBEFORE** gives everything before a character, **TEXTAFTER** gives everything after it. No counting, no `-1`.

Press **Play** to watch one being built. Older Excel versions don't have these, so keep the FIND recipe in mind.

frames.label: Click the cell for the answer
Type =TEXTBEFORE( and click the text: A2
Add a comma and the character to cut at, in quotes

steps.prompt: Your turn. In ==B2==, type `=TEXTBEFORE(A2,"@")` to get the part of the email before the `@`.
steps.explain: **meera.** One function replaced `LEFT(A2,FIND("@",A2)-1)`. The `@` goes in quotes because it's text you're looking for.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Put the `@` in quotes after a comma: `=TEXTBEFORE(A2,"@")`.

clues: If your Excel says #NAME?, it's an older version without this function.

steps.prompt:
Same idea, other direction. **TEXTAFTER** gives everything **after** the character.

In ==B2==, get the website part of the first email (after the `@`).
steps.explain: **mailbox.com.** TEXTAFTER keeps everything to the right of the first `@`. Together, TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER split any text in two.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the quotes around `@`.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `TEXTAFTER` for the part that comes after.

steps.prompt:
Order codes have **two** dashes. A plain TEXTAFTER cuts at the **first** dash. An optional third argument picks which one: `2` means the second dash.

In ==B2==, get just the number part of `KOL-2025-0733`: everything after the **second** dash.
steps.explain: **0733.** With just `"-"`, you'd get “2025-0733”, everything after the first dash. The `2` made Excel skip to the second one. (`-1` counts from the end instead, handy when you always want the last piece.)

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets, quotes and commas: `=TEXTAFTER(A2,"-",2)`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You want only what follows the **second** dash: add `,2` after the dash.

steps.text:
**TEXTSPLIT** cuts text at every separator and puts each piece in its **own cell**, in one go. You type it in one cell and the results **spill** to the right.

In Excel you'd type `=TEXTSPLIT(A2,",")` in ==B2== and press Enter. Excel fills ==B2:D2== by itself. Same for row 3.

This practice sheet can't run TEXTSPLIT, so here's what Excel shows. Like TEXTBEFORE, it needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024.

steps.prompt:
`A2` holds `Asha,Pune,Sales`. You type `=TEXTSPLIT(A2,",")` in ==B2== and press Enter.

What ends up in ==C2==, the cell next to the formula, which you never typed in?
steps.explain: **Pune.** The first piece (Asha) lands in B2, and the rest **spill** into C2 and D2. You only wrote one formula, but it fills three cells. Spilling is why those cells must stay free.
wrongFeedback: That's how most formulas behave, but TEXTSPLIT returns several values, one per cell.
It splits at each comma, so every piece is separate.
clues: How many pieces does the text have? Where do they go?

steps.prompt:
You type `=TEXTSPLIT(A2,",")` in `B2`, but `D2` already has the word **Leave** typed in it.

What does Excel show in `B2`?
options: Asha and Pune, and it overwrites `D2`
Asha, Pune and Sales, with `Leave` pushed right
steps.explain: **`#SPILL!`.** Excel won't overwrite your data. Clear `D2` (or move the formula somewhere with room) and the pieces appear. Hover the error's warning sign to see which cell is in the way.
wrongFeedback: Excel never overwrites typed cells for you. It stops and shows an error instead.
Excel doesn't push data aside. It warns you.
clues: What does Excel do when something is in the way?

steps.prompt:
Now the opposite job: **gluing** a list together. **TEXTJOIN** takes three things: the **separator**, whether to **skip blanks** (TRUE), and the **range**.

In ==B2==, type `=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:A6)` to list the volunteers on one line.
steps.explain: **Asha, Ben, Chitra, Dev, Esha.** The separator `", "` (comma and space) went between every pair of names. Great for invite lists and email “To” lines.
clues: The separator is a comma and a space, in quotes.

steps.prompt:
One volunteer cell is empty. The middle argument decides what happens: **TRUE** skips blank cells; **FALSE** leaves a double separator where each blank was.

In ==B2==, join the names with ` / ` between them and **no gaps**.
steps.explain: **Kavya / Rohan / Neha / Zoya.** TRUE skipped the empty `A4`. With FALSE you'd see “Rohan /  / Neha” with an empty slot in the middle.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the quotes around the separator, then TRUE, then the range.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Use ` / ` as the separator (spaces included) and TRUE to skip the empty cell.

clues: Which value skips blanks: TRUE or FALSE?

steps.prompt:
For just **two or three** pieces, `&` is quicker than TEXTJOIN. It glues text together, but it adds nothing on its own, so **you** supply the space: a space in quotes.

In ==C2==, join First and Last into `Anil Kapoor`.
steps.explain: **Anil Kapoor.** `A2&" "&B2` glues three things: the first name, a space, the last name. Forget the space and you get “AnilKapoor”.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the quotes around the space: `" "`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Glue first name, a space in quotes, then last name: `=A2&" "&B2`. Missing the space gives “AnilKapoor”.

steps.prompt:
TEXTBEFORE shows `#N/A` when the character it's looking for **isn't there**. Row 3 has no email, so ==B3== shows an error.

Change ==B3== so it shows the original text (`not provided`) when there's no `@`. You met the tool for this in Topic 25.
steps.explain: **not provided.** IFERROR tries TEXTBEFORE first, and if it fails, shows `A3` instead. Real lists always have a few rows that don't fit the pattern.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Wrap the TEXTBEFORE so that an error falls back to the original text in `A3`.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Keep `TEXTBEFORE` in your formula and wrap it.

clues: What should it show instead? The original text, `A3`.

steps.prompt:
Last one, from memory.

The event sheet lists each guest as `Kavya Rao | Pune`: name, a bar, then the city. In ==B2==, show just the **city**, with no extra space at the front.
steps.explain: **Pune.** The separator can be longer than one character: `" | "` includes its spaces, so nothing is left over. Cutting at just `"|"` leaves a leading space, which `TRIM` could also remove.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Take what comes after the bar, but watch for a stray space at the front of the city.

clues: The bar `|` has spaces around it in the text.
Either include the spaces in the separator, or tidy up afterwards.
